x: Lory Lory is a UI and graphics library for Crow . A Crow program built for the web is WebAssembly that draws everything itself with WebGL2: controls, forms, tables, charts, maps, 3D scenes, sound and games. The same program runs in a page, on a phone and in a VR or AR headset. The site: agncrow.github.io/lory has a guide to every part of Lory and every example running live. Packages Package use What it gives you packages/lory lory , lory.gui , lory.forms , lory.datatable , lory.space , … The renderer, the controls and the components, 3D, and the headset packages/kite kite , kite.charts Charts: lines, bars, pies, scatter and more, and financial charts packages/map map Maps of tiles with markers, popups, shapes and clusters packages/sound sound Synths, effects, a sequencer and analysers, rendered in Crow packages/window window A window of panels standing around the reader in a headset packages/game game A fixed-rate clock, collisions, sparks and sounds A first program use sys use lory use lory.gui fn draw[frame] c = lory.begin[frame] c = lory.clear[c, gui.dark[].page] shown = gui.show[c, gui.panel[[gui.heading['Hello'], gui.button['wave', 'Wave']]]] for e in shown.events if e.id eq 'wave' log['waved'] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] Clone this repository beside your project. Name its packages in your crowfile, for example deps = map[lory = '../lory/packages/lory'] , then run crow install . Run crow build --target web main.co and serve main_web/ over HTTP. A view is a tree rebuilt from the program's state every frame. Lory keeps what the controls hold between frames, such as the focus, a field's caret and which menus are open. The program reads what the reader did as events. What is in it Controls: buttons, fields, sliders, toggles, checkboxes, radios, tabs, selects, tables, layers, tips, roving focus and themes. Colours, icons and motion: colour scales and themes, an icon set, and easings, springs and timelines. Forms: validation, masks, comboboxes, ratings, code inputs, a Markdown editor and a drawing pad. Menus and overlays: menubars, context menus, a command palette, dialogs, drawers, popovers, tooltips, notifications, accordions and trees. Navigation and display: app bars, breadcrumbs, steppers, pagination, cards, chips, avatars, badges, timelines, skeletons and spinners. Dates and times: date, range, month, year and time pickers, and a calendar with month, week and day views. Data: a data table (search, sort, pages, groups) and a data grid (editing, ranges, a live feed, a spreadsheet). Charts, carousels, scrolling, drag and drop, maps, 3D, model files and sound. Every part works in a headset: the controller's ray points and presses, the trigger drags, the thumbstick scrolls, and a keyboard is drawn for typing. Examples examples/ holds programs that each build for the web. The site runs them live. Testing ./test.sh runs every package's tests, in both of Crow's modes (interpreted and compiled), builds every example for the web, drives the examples in headless Chrome, and walks the 3D and headset examples in a made-up headset. How Lory works A view is a tree, drawn every frame A Lory program answers each frame. It builds a tree of controls from its state, such as a column holding a heading, a field and a button. Lory lays the tree out, draws it and tells the program what the reader did as events. Then the program changes its state, and the next frame shows the change. Lory keeps what the controls themselves hold between frames: the focus, a field's caret and selection, how far a list is scrolled, which menus are open. A program keeps only its own data. use sys use lory use lory.gui use memory struct Counter [count] fn draw[frame] c = lory.begin[frame] count = recall['counter', Counter[0]].count shown = gui.show[c, gui.panel[[gui.heading['Clicked `count` times'], gui.button['more', 'Click']]]] for e in shown.events if e.id eq 'more' count = count + 1 remember['counter', Counter[count]] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] Everything is drawn A program built with crow build --target web is WebAssembly. Each frame it hands the page one batch of WebGL2 calls, and the page runs them. Every control, chart, map and scene is drawn by Lory itself, so a page looks and behaves the same in every browser and in a headset. Text is drawn from a font atlas that stays sharp at any size and in a headset. The layers Layer What it holds Renderer Buffers, shaders, one batch of drawing a frame Controls ( lory.gui ) Every control, layout, focus, scrolling and hit testing Components Forms, menus, tables, pickers, carousels and the rest, built from the controls Charts ( kite ) Scales, axes, legends and marks of every kind 3D ( lory.space ) Shapes, cameras, materials, lights and shadows Headset ( lory.xr ) Both eyes, controllers as pointer rays, panels placed in the room Fast by design Work in proportion to what changed. The GPU does the work for each vertex. Crow code runs once for each change. One batch a frame. The program hands the page one batch of drawing a frame, not thousands of calls. Draw what a pixel can show. A long series is reduced to what each column of pixels can show before it is drawn. The headset's budget. A headset runs at 72 to 120 frames a second, so both eyes are drawn in one pass. Both of Crow's modes Crow runs a program interpreted ( crow run -i ) or compiled ( crow run , crow build ). Lory's tests run in both, and their answers are the same.

x: In a headset: VR and AR Everything Lory draws runs in a headset as it runs on a screen. Nothing is rebuilt for VR or AR: Lory reads a headset's controllers as it reads a mouse, so every control, chart, map and scene works there. Entering a headset A page built with crow build --target web enters a headset in one of two ways: The page's own buttons. Enter VR shows where a headset can be entered, and Enter AR where one can show the room through the drawing. A button the program draws. When it is pressed, the program paints [["@vr"]] or [["@ar"]] . A browser enters only on the reader's press. If none can be entered, a later frame says so. Each frame tells the program where it is: Field What it says xr A headset shows this frame vr A headset can be entered ar A headset can be entered with the room seen through the drawing blend What is behind the drawing: opaque on a screen and in VR, alpha-blend or additive in AR How things behave Where the page is. The page is drawn on a panel 2 m wide, 1.5 m ahead of the reader, with its top 1.8 m up. A program can instead stand several panels around the reader ( lory.xr 's room, and the window package). Pointing and pressing. A controller's ray is the pointer where it meets the panel, and its trigger presses. The trigger held while the ray moves drags: sliders, sortable lists, carousels, maps and cards. The ray resting on a control is a hover, so hover states light up and tips show. A dot marks where the ray meets the panel. Scrolling. The thumbstick scrolls what the ray rests on, as a wheel does on a screen: lists, tables, scroll areas and sideways carousels. Typing. A headset's browser shows no keyboard over an immersive page, so Lory draws one under the field that has the focus, its keys pressed by the ray. Menus and dialogs are drawn on the panel over the page, placed as on a screen. 3D scenes stand around the reader. The ray picks things, and the sticks walk and turn. AR: the room seen through In AR, lory.seen_through[c] is true, and Lory clears each frame to transparent, whatever colour the program asked for. The room shows wherever nothing is drawn. Panels, cards and controls keep their own fills, so they stand in the room as solid things. A program in AR should draw no backdrop that would hide the room. A 3D scene should leave out its ground, so its things stand on the reader's own floor. Trying it without a headset Lory Studio ( studio/ ) is a made-up headset in a desktop browser. It walks a program as a headset would (entering, pointing, looking about, walking) and compares each picture with the one kept for it.

Controls lory.gui is the set of controls every other part of Lory is built from. A view is a tree your program rebuilds from its own state each frame: columns and rows, words, buttons, fields, sliders, toggles, tabs, a table. gui.show lays the tree out, draws it on the canvas and answers it from the frame's input in one pass, handing back the events of that frame. What a control holds between frames (the focus, a field's caret and selection, a scroll, which layers are open) Lory keeps; what it shows is yours. Every control answers the pointer, touch and the keyboard. Tab and Shift-Tab move the focus, with a ring on the focused control; a button is pressed by Enter or Space; arrows move within a group, a slider or a field; Escape closes the top layer. Components Component What it does Column, row, grid, panel Lay controls one above another, side by side, in equal columns, or on a raised card Header An app bar: a raised row with an edge under it Scroll area A column of a fixed height whose controls scroll by wheel, drag or thumbstick Overlay One control drawn over another at one of nine anchors, such as a badge Text, heading, label, note Words at the type scale's sizes, in a tone: ink, muted, accent, danger, success or warning Button Pressed by the pointer, Enter or Space Item A row pressed as one: an entry of a list, a menu or a card Text field and text area Typed in at a caret, with selection, copy and paste; text, password or number Slider Dragged, or stepped by the arrows, Page Up and Down, Home and End Toggle and checkbox A switch and a ticked box; a checkbox may be mixed Radio group, tabs, select One choice of several, chosen by press or arrows Disclosure A summary that shows and hides what follows it Progress bar Determinate, or going on with no known end Table Rows of text under a header, a row chosen by press Drawn control A box your program paints in the tree's own pass, pressed, dragged and keyed like any other Layer Anything drawn over the rest: placed against a control or at a place of the page Dropdown A button that opens a panel under it Modal A dialog in the middle of a dimmed page that keeps the focus Drawer A panel along a side of the page Toast A notice that closes itself after its time, paused while the pointer rests on it Tip Words over a control once the pointer has rested on it Roving group A set of controls that is one Tab stop, the arrows moving among them Layers and focus A layer is drawn after the tree, over everything, and takes no room where it stands. Placed against a control, it goes on a side (top, bottom, left or right), aligned along it, and flips to the other side or shifts along when the page has no room. Placed at the page, it stands in the middle, at an edge or a corner, or where the pointer last pressed. A modal layer blocks what is under it, keeps Tab among its own controls and can dim the page. A layer the reader may dismiss closes on Escape or a press outside it, and tells how it was closed. A focused layer takes the focus as it opens and gives it back as it closes. Controls can be moved, faded or scaled as they are drawn ( gui.moved , gui.faded , gui.scaled ); the pointer finds them where they are drawn, which is what lory.motion 's tweens and springs drive. A disabled control is dimmed and passed over by Tab and the pointer. Themes gui.dark[] and gui.light[] give a look: page, panel, edge, ink, muted, accent and the colours of states. lory.colors makes a look's colours from any accent and gray. gui.show_at takes two more sizes for a theme: scale sizes every control, its words and its gaps (0.9 to 1.1 suits most pages) without changing the room it is given, and radius times every corner, 0 for square and large for pills. Words in an accent tone are moved toward black or white until they read on their panel. Using it use sys use memory use lory use lory.gui struct App [name, volume, loud, fruit, presses] fn settings[a] form = gui.panel[[gui.heading['Settings'], gui.label['Your name'], gui.field['name', a.name], gui.label['Volume'], gui.slider['volume', a.volume, 0.0, 1.0], gui.toggle['loud', 'Loud', a.loud], gui.select['fruit', ['apple', 'pear', 'plum'], a.fruit], gui.button['press', 'Press me'], gui.note['Pressed `a.presses` times']]] gui.column[[form], pad = 24.0] fn draw[frame] a = recall['app', App['Ada', 0.4, false, 'pear', 0]] c = lory.begin[frame] shown = gui.show[c, settings[a]] for e in shown.events if e.id eq 'name' and e.act eq 'edit' a.name = e.words if e.id eq 'volume' a.volume = e.num if e.id eq 'loud' a.loud = e.num gt 0.5 if e.id eq 'fruit' a.fruit = e.words if e.id eq 'press' and e.act eq 'press' a.presses = a.presses + 1 remember['app', a] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] Each event names its control's id and what happened ( press , edit , change , choose , toggle , dismiss ), with its words and number. In a headset The page stands on a panel in the room. The controller's ray points and presses as the pointer does, and the thumbstick of the hand whose ray rests on a scroll area turns it. Colours and themes lory.colors is Lory's colour module. A colour is a lory.Color : its sRGB channels and its opacity, each from 0 to 1. The module reads and writes hex codes, moves colours between linear light, OKLab, OKLCH, HSL and HSV, mixes two colours in any of those spaces, makes a colour lighter, darker or more saturated and fits it back inside sRGB, and lays a translucent colour over another. It measures text on a background two ways: by contrast ratio (1 to 21) and by lightness contrast (Lc, signed: positive for dark text on light). It also makes colour scales of its own: 31 named scales of twelve steps, six grays and 25 accents, each in a light and a dark appearance, solid and translucent. Each step has a role (1 the page, 2 a subtle background, 3 to 5 a control at rest, hovered and pressed, 6 to 8 borders and the focus ring, 9 and 10 solid fills, 11 and 12 text), and the two text steps keep at least Lc 60 and Lc 90 on their scale's first two steps. From the scales come a theme's tokens, which a program turns into the look it draws with. The module draws nothing itself. Components Component What it does Hex codes parse reads #rgb , #rgba , #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa ; hex_of and hex_alpha_of write them Colour spaces to_oklab , to_oklch , to_hsl , to_hsv , to_linear and back; oklch makes a colour fitted inside sRGB Mixing mix blends two colours in any space, hues the shorter way round Moving a colour lighter , darker , saturated , fitted Laying over over lays a translucent colour on another; translucent finds the least opaque colour that gives a solid one Contrast luminance , contrast_ratio , contrast_lc , and on_color for white or black text on a colour Scales scale and step give a scale's solid steps; alpha_scale its translucent ones; black_overlay and white_overlay twelve steps of each Custom scale scale_from makes a full scale with your brand colour as its step 9 Pairing gray_for gives the gray that goes with an accent; on_solid the text on a scale's solid steps Named colours Thirteen named colours with their hover, focus, pressed and active shades Palette 22 named colours, each with lighter, darker and accent shades Theme theme gives a page, panel, edges, ink, accent, a control's states, focus ring, overlay, shadow and four status colours for an accent, a gray and an appearance Using it use sys use lory use lory.gui use lory.colors fn look_of[t] look = gui.light[] look.page = t.page look.panel = t.panel look.edge = t.edge look.ink = t.ink look.muted = t.muted look.accent = t.accent look.on_accent = t.on_accent look.focus = t.focus look fn draw[frame] t = colors.theme['indigo', 'auto', 'light'] lc = colors.contrast_lc[t.ink, t.page] brand = colors.scale_from[colors.parse['#7c3aed'], 'light'] c = lory.begin[frame] tree = gui.panel[[gui.heading['A theme'], gui.note['Ink on the page: Lc `fmt[lc, decimals = 1]`'], gui.button['go', 'Go']]] shown = gui.show_at[c, tree, 24.0, 24.0, 360.0, look_of[t]] c = lory.rect[shown.canvas, 24.0, 300.0, 48.0, 48.0, brand[8]] lory.end[c] sys.frames[draw] A scale is a list of twelve colours, step 1 first, so brand[8] is step 9. colors.theme takes auto for the gray paired with the accent, or any gray by name, and dark for the dark appearance. In a headset Colours are the same on a panel in the room as on a page; a theme's look draws the panels a headset shows. Try it Open the colours example

Icons lory.icons draws icons by name, at any size and in one colour, from Lory's own lines, discs, rings and boxes. There are about four hundred names: every glyph a control needs (check, chevrons, arrows, search, menu, settings, a loader), a broad general set (alignment, borders, text styles, layout, files, people, media, devices) and the icons other parts of Lory ask for (a table's sorts, a map's pins, a player's keys, an editor's lists, a hotkey's keys). A name is written with hyphens or underscores, so eye-off and eye_off are the same icon, and a few common words are other names' drawings ( close is x ). A name the set does not draw is drawn as a small outlined square. Each icon is designed on a grid of 15 units and scaled to the square it is drawn in. Its strokes are one unit wide with round ends and corners, so an icon drawn 15 pixels wide from a whole pixel has crisp one-pixel lines. Solid shapes (play, a filled star) are filled and edged with the same stroke. Components Component What it does Icon icons.draw draws a named icon in a square at a size and colour Turned icon icons.turned turns it about its middle, such as a section's chevron as it opens Spinning icon icons.spinning turns a loading icon once every two seconds by the frame's time Flipped icon icons.flipped mirrors it horizontally or vertically Names icons.names lists every name drawn; icons.known says whether a name is Using it use sys use lory use lory.icons fn draw[frame] c = lory.begin[frame] c = lory.clear[c, lory.white[]] ink = lory.black[] c = icons.draw[c, 'check', 24.0, 24.0, 24.0, ink] c = icons.draw[c, 'magnifying-glass', 64.0, 24.0, 24.0, ink] c = icons.turned[c, 'chevron-right', 104.0, 24.0, 24.0, ink, 90.0] c = icons.flipped[c, 'arrow-right', 144.0, 24.0, 24.0, ink, 'horizontally'] c = icons.spinning[c, 'loader', 184.0, 24.0, 24.0, ink, lory.time[c]] lory.end[c] sys.frames[draw] Strokes overlap where an icon's parts meet, so draw an icon in an opaque colour (mix it with what is behind it with lory.mix ) rather than a translucent one. In a headset An icon is drawn on a panel in the room just as on a page, in both eyes. Try it Open the icons example Not included yet Brand logos

Motion lory.motion moves things: easings, springs, throws that slow to a stop, animations kept between frames, timelines, staggers, and the arithmetic of scroll-driven effects. An easing is named by its text, so a program can write 'outQuad' , 'inOutBack(2)' , 'outElastic(1, .3)' , 'easeInOut' , 'ease-in-out' , 'cubic-bezier(.68,-.55,.265,1.55)' , 'steps(5, jump-both)' , 'linear(0, 0.6 30%, 1)' or 'spring(1, 120, 9, 0)' . A name it does not know is linear. An animation held between frames is your program's definition (what moves, for how long, with which easing), handed in each frame, and Lory's clock for it, kept under an id and read against the frame's time. A new target starts a tween again from where the value stands, and a spring from where it is at the speed it has, so motion never jumps. A clock can be paused, resumed, reversed, sought, sped up and restarted. The values drive what is drawn: a control moved, faded or scaled with gui.moved , gui.faded and gui.scaled , or anything a program paints. Components Component What it does Easings Named curves in families (quad, cubic, quart, quint, sine, circ, expo, bounce, back, elastic) turned in, out, in-out and out-in; cubic béziers, steps, points and irregular curves Spring A spring by its stiffness, damping and mass, or by how long it takes and how much it bounces Throw A value let go at a speed, slowing to rest, caught by a spring at its bounds and snapped to a step Tween A value easing to a target, kept between frames Keyframes Several values over a time, each stretch with its own easing Clock An animation's playback: delay, repeats, pauses between, alternate direction, speed Presence A value from 0 to 1 that enters while something is shown and leaves once it is hidden, turning where it stands if changed half way Timeline Children placed one after another, at offsets ( '-=300' ), labels ( 'turn' ) or beside the one before ( '<' , '<<+=200' ) Stagger Delays across a list or a grid, from the first, the last, the centre, the edges, a point or a random order Scroll progress How far a target has come through its container, by offsets that meet the two's edges Scroll window Where a target's scroll-driven progress starts and ends Reveal line The scroll at which an element is revealed, by its anchor placement Motion path A point and its heading along a line of points, and the line drawn so far Text split A line split into words or characters to stagger Number helpers Damp, blend, map from one range to another, wrap, snap and a seeded random Using it use sys use memory use lory use lory.gui use lory.motion struct Page In a headset Motion runs on the frame's time in a headset as on a page, so a spring or a timeline plays at the same pace on a panel in the room. Try it Open the motion example

Forms, validation and editors lory.forms gives you the controls a form is made of, beyond gui's own buttons, fields and checkboxes, and the rules a form is checked by. lory.editors adds a Markdown editor with a live preview and an image editor. Each control is built from lory.gui and placed in a tree like gui's own controls; your program keeps the values, and Lory keeps the rest (focus, words being typed, a slider being dragged). Every control works by keyboard, pointer and touch. Tab moves between controls, and the arrows move within a group or a slider, with Home and End going to the ends. Enter and space press, toggle or choose, and Escape closes a combobox's list. A form is checked when its submit button is pressed or Enter is typed in a field. The first field that fails gets the focus, and each field's first failed rule is shown under it. After that, a field in error is checked again as it is typed in. Menus, dialogs and notifications Three modules hold what opens over a page or under a trigger. lory.menus gives dropdown and context menus, a menubar, a navigation menu, a command palette and a floating action button with its speed dial. lory.overlays gives dialogs, popovers, hover cards, tooltips, toasts and snackbars, sheets, banners and dimmers. lory.disclosure gives the accordion, the collapsible and the tree view. Everything answers the keyboard, the pointer and touch. Menus move with the arrows, Home and End, type ahead by first letters, and close on Escape or a press outside; a submenu opens after a short rest and stays open while the pointer heads for it. A context menu opens on a right press or a touch held 700 ms. Dialogs keep the focus and give it back when they close. Toasts pause while the pointer is on them, close on a swipe, and F8 takes the focus to the newest. Your program keeps what is open (a dialog's open , the folds open, the notices shown) and changes it on the events each frame tells; Lory keeps the small things inside, such as a menu's highlighted row, a tooltip's timers and a tree's open folders. Navigation and display Two modules hold what takes a reader around a program and what a page shows. lory.navigation gives app bars, system bars and footers, bottom navigation, breadcrumbs, menu bars, navigation buttons, pagination, steppers and toolbars. lory.display gives avatars, badges, cards, chips, lists, data lists, timelines, feeds and comments, skeletons, spinners and circular progress, key caps and shortcuts, inline text styles, empty states, statistics, alerts and callouts, images, galleries with a lightbox, highlighted words and advertisement slots. A toolbar, a menu bar, a chip group, a list, a gallery and bottom navigation are each one stop of Tab: the arrows move along them (round, where they loop), Home and End go to the ends, and Enter or space presses. Every part answers a press of the mouse or a touch. None changes what it shows by itself: your program keeps the page, the step and the chips chosen, and draws the component again from the events it told. Lory keeps the small things, such as the crumbs opened, an avatar's first frame, an alert's time shown and the images loaded. ellipsis that opens it Menu bar Entries along a bar, or one under another, with a dropdown entry Navigation button A destination of a rail, a drawer or a bottom bar, with a badge Pagination Arrows and a run of pages about the one shown, fitted to a width Windowed pagination First, previous, "more", page, next and last buttons over windows of pages Stepper Numbered steps, linear or editable, with Back and Continue; a vertical stepper too Toolbar Buttons, toggles, a group of toggles, separators and links along a bar Avatar and avatar group A picture in a circle, its initials until it loads; several overlapping Badge A small label, or a count or dot over a control's corner Card A title, subtitle and words on a raised ground, pressed as one Chip and chip group Tags and filters, closable, one or many chosen List Entries with icons, titles and subtitles; groups that open; numbered entries Data list Labels beside what they hold Timeline Events in order on a line, alternating sides or along it Feed and comment Events and comments with initials, times and replies Skeleton and placeholder Shapes that pulse or shimmer while content loads Spinner, dots and loader Indicators that Dates, times and calendars Lory's date and time controls come in two modules. lory.calendar is the arithmetic of days, dates written in a locale's words and read back from words, the rules for which days may be chosen, a month's calendar drawn as one control, and a scheduler. lory.pickers puts them in a field: a day, a range, several days, a week, a month, a quarter, a year (and ranges of them), a time, or a day and a time, each with its calendar or list in a layer under the field, or inline without one. Your program holds what is chosen, a list of moments; Lory holds the rest under the picker's id (the month shown, the day the keys move from, the words being typed, whether the calendar is open). A press on the field opens the calendar, and words typed are read by the field's pattern as you type. In the calendar the arrow keys move a day or a week, Page Up and Page Down a month (with Shift a year), Home and End to the week's first and last day, Enter and space choose and Escape closes; days that may not be chosen are stepped past. A choice that ends (a day, a week, a range's last day) closes the calendar and gives the focus back to the field. A list of times scrolls by the wheel or a trackpad and is keyed through with the arrows. Components Component What it does Date field A day typed or chosen from a calendar that opens under the field Range field A first and a last day, the days to the pointer shaded, over one or more months Multiple dates Days added and taken away by pressing, written a, b or a (+n) Week, month, quarter and year fields A period chosen from its tiles or its calendar, and ranges of months, quarters and years Time field A time from a list at a set step, or typed and stepped by Up and Down Date and time field A day from the calendar and its time from the list beside it Inline calendar Any of the above without its field, always shown Month calendar One or several months side by side, with weekday names, week numbers, tones and holidays Scheduler A month, week or day of entries, overlapping ones side by side and whole days in lanes Date rules Earliest and latest days, days and spans left out or only allowed, a filter, tones and holidays Date formats Moments written and read by patterns such as MM/dd/yyyy , EEEE, MMMM do and h:mm aa , in en-US, en-GB, fr, de and es, in any zone Using it use sys use memory use lory use lory.gui use lory.calendar use lory.pickers fn due_of[] p = pickers.with_icon[pickers.date_picker['due']] p = pickers.clearable[pickers.with_today[p, 'Today']] pickers.ruled[p, calendar.bounded[calendar.rules[], calendar.day[2026, 1, 1], calendar.day[2026, 12, 31]]] struct App [due] fn draw[frame] a = recall['app', App[[calendar.day[2026, 7, 14]]]] c = lory.begin[frame] tree = gui.column[[gui.label['Due'], pickers.control[due_of[], a.due]]] shown = gui.show[c, tree] a.due = pickers.answered[due_of[], a.due, shown] remember['app', a] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] Days are moments at midnight in UTC ( calendar.day[2024, 3, 5] ), so they compare and subtract as moments do. calendar.add_months[calendar.day[2024, 1, 31], 1] is 2024-02-29, and calendar.format[t, 'yyyy-MM-dd', calendar.locale['en-US']] writes a day. In a headset Calendars, lists and the scheduler are drawn on the page as on a screen and pressed by a controller's ray as by a mouse; a thumbstick scrolls the list of times. A field typed in brings up Lory's drawn keyboard, but choosing by pressing needs no keyboard at all. Carousels and sliders lory.carousel moves slides, and the slides are any of Lory's controls. A carousel is moved by its arrows and dots, by the arrow keys while it has the focus, by a swipe (touch, the mouse where it is draggable, a headset's ray) and by autoplay, which pauses while the pointer rests on it. It shows one slide or several, wraps round or stops at its ends, and its settings can change with the page's width. Beside it are a window of panes, a slide group of chips and an endless ticker. What a carousel holds between frames (the slide shown, a move under way, a swipe, autoplay's clock) is Lory's, kept under its id; the slides and the settings are your program's, handed to it each frame. What the reader does comes back as events under the carousel's id: change as a move begins and settle as it ends, with swipe , edge and load . Components Component What it does Carousel Slides moved by arrows, dots, keys, swipes and autoplay, one at a time or several, wrapping or not Centred carousel The slide shown in the middle, its neighbours peeking Variable width and adaptive height Each slide as wide as it is; the carousel as tall as the slide shown Fade Slides fading over one another instead of sliding Vertical and right to left Slides one above another, swiped up and down; or the order and arrows reversed Rows Slides grouped into a grid of rows, the group moved as one Lazy loading Slides drawn only as they come near Breakpoints Other settings below a page width, or the slides simply stacked Linked carousels Two carousels that move each other, such as a picture and its thumbnails Window One pane at a time, the next sliding in the way its index goes Slide group A row of chips wider than its room, scrolled a page at a time, a chosen chip scrolled into view Ticker An endless line of items, slowed while hovered, dragged and thrown Using it use sys use lory use lory.gui use lory.carousel fn slide[n] gui.panel[[gui.heading['Slide `n`'], gui.space[120.0]]] fn draw[frame] c = lory.begin[frame] slides = [slide[1], slide[2], slide[3], slide[4], slide[5], slide[6]] s = carousel.settings[show = 3, scroll = 3, dots = true, autoplay = true] shown = gui.show[c, gui.column[[carousel.carousel[c, 'hero', slides, s]]]] for ev in shown.events if ev.id eq 'hero' and ev.act eq 'settle' log['showing slide `ev.num`'] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] A program moves a carousel itself with carousel.next_slide , carousel.previous_slide , carousel.go_to , carousel.play and carousel.pause , and gives it settings for page widths with carousel.breakpoint and carousel.responsive . In a headset The ray presses the arrows and dots, and holding the trigger while the ray moves swipes a carousel, a window or a slide group. Try it Open the carousels example Not included yet Scrolling a carousel or ticker by the wheel Progress bars and masked edges

Scrolling and parallax lory.scrolling covers what a page does as it scrolls, and the scrolling itself: full-page sections, a scroll area with its own bar, virtual lists that draw only the rows in view, endless feeds, pull to refresh, reveals on scroll, smooth scrolling, scroll-linked progress, sticky blocks, parallax, visibility events and a scroll spy. Each is arithmetic on numbers your program holds (scroll positions, box tops and heights in CSS pixels, times in milliseconds), and the parts that draw are built of Lory's controls. Full-page sections move by the arrow keys, Page Up and Page Down, Home and End, Space, the wheel, a swipe and their navigation dots; a scroll area scrolls by the wheel, the keys, dragging its thumb or pressing its track. Components Component What it does Full-page sections A page cut into sections moved one at a time, with dots, anchors in the address, loops, slides across with arrows, sections taller than the page and lazy media Scroll area A view with its own bar, shown on hover (or while scrolling, or always) and hidden 600 ms after Virtual list and grid Only the rows and columns near the view drawn, each measured as it is drawn, for lists of any length Endless feed More asked for as an edge comes near or a button is pressed, with loading, done and error states Pull to refresh Content pulled down from the top, refreshing once let go past its threshold Reveal on scroll Elements fading, sliding, zooming or flipping in as they come into view, once or each time Smooth scrolling A wheel's scroll eased frame by frame, and a scroll to a place over a time Scroll-linked progress A value moved by how far a target has passed through the view, or the page's own progress Sticky A block that stays in view while its part scrolls past, and lets go at its end Parallax A picture or a layer moving slower or faster than the page Visibility Told as a block comes into view, passes or leaves, and loaded once seen Scroll spy Which part of the page is in view, for a table of contents Using it use sys use memory use lory use lory.gui use lory.scrolling fn sections[] [scrolling.section[name = 'one'], scrolling.section[name = 'two', slides = 2], scrolling.section[name = 'three']] fn faces[] [gui.heading['One'], gui.heading['Two: the first slide'], gui.heading['Two: the second slide'], gui.heading['Three']] fn draw[frame] c = lory.begin[frame] p = recall['pages', scrolling.pages[sections[], 800.0, 500.0, scrolling.page_options[nav = true]]] p = scrolling.paged[c, p] --- the keys, the wheel, the time shown = gui.show[c, scrolling.pages_view[p, faces[]]] p = scrolling.pages_heard[p, shown] --- its dots and arrows pressed for e in p.told if e.name eq 'after_load' log['now on section `e.section`'] remember['pages', p] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] Faces are listed in section order, with one face for each slide of a section that has slides. A scroll area goes the same way: scrolling.area_scrolled[c, a] , then scrolling.area_view[a, id, tall, rows] in the tree, then scrolling.area_heard[a, shown, id] . In a headset The thumbstick scrolls whatever the ray rests on, and the ray presses the dots, arrows and bars. Drag and drop lory.drag reorders lists by dragging and carries items between them, and has the drags that are not a list's: a control dragged freely and thrown, a stack of cards swiped away, a row swiped open to show its actions, a slider that compares two pictures, two fingers that zoom, turn and pan, and a honeycomb of icons dragged and zoomed. Draw your tree with drag.show in place of gui.show . What the reader does comes back as events ( start , move , change , add , remove , sort , end and the rest), and your program takes each end into its own lists ( drag.after does it for lists of ids). Items are dragged by mouse, touch or pen, by a grip where the list asks for one; a list in a group takes items from the others, and can clone, swap, take several at once, scroll its area near an edge, and wait for a delay before a touch drag starts. Components Component What it does Sortable list A column, row or grid of items reordered by dragging, its items sliding into place Shared lists Lists in a group carrying items between them, or cloning them from a palette Swap An item let go over another trading places with it Several at once Items selected by pressing (with Shift, Ctrl or Cmd) and dragged together Grip and filter Items dragged only by their grip, or some items not dragged at all Free drag A control dragged within bounds, pulled past them elastically, thrown on at its speed, snapped home or locked to an axis Swipe cards A stack of cards swiped left or right and away Swipe actions A row swiped open to show its actions Compare slider A divider dragged across one picture laid over another Pinch Two fingers (or Ctrl and the wheel) zooming, turning and panning a picture Honeycomb A field of icons dragged about and zoomed Using it use sys use memory use lory use lory.gui use lory.drag struct App [lists] fn items_of[ids] out = slice[[gui.space[0.0]], 0, 0] for id in ids out = push[out, gui.item[id, [gui.text[id]]]] out fn draw[frame] a = recall['app', App[map['todo' = ['Write', 'Test', 'Ship'], 'done' = ['Plan']]]] c = lory.begin[frame] todo = drag.grouped[drag.list['todo', items_of[a.lists['todo']]], 'tasks'] done = drag.grouped[drag.list['done', items_of[a.lists['done']]], 'tasks'] shown = drag.show[c, gui.row[[gui.sized[todo, 300.0], gui.sized[done, 300.0]], gap = 20.0]] for t in shown.told if t.act eq 'end' a.lists = drag.after[a.lists, t] remember['app', a] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] In a headset The controller's ray presses an item and its trigger carries it, the same as a mouse; a free control or a card is thrown by moving the ray and letting go. Try it Open the drag and drop example

Data table lory.datatable is the row model behind a table: plain functions over rows of cells and column definitions, with nothing drawn. It sorts (by one column or several, with six sort functions and a press that cycles ascending, descending and off), filters (column filters, a global search, fuzzy ranks and facets), groups rows and sums them up, expands sub-rows, pages, selects and pins rows, and orders, hides, pins, sizes and resizes columns under header groups. A simpler grid with a search field, a sort cycle and page buttons with their words is there too. A table is a record your program holds: its columns, its rows, its options and its state. Each change answers the table changed (a new filter goes back to the first page), and models works out the rows to draw once. Draw them with gui's table , or with any controls you like; the data grid stands on the same tables. Presses, Shift-presses (a sort of several columns), typing and the keys are the drawing's, so a table works the same by mouse, touch and keyboard. Components Component What it does Sorting One column or several, by text, numbers, dates or the fuzzy rank, missing values placed first or last Filters and search A filter per column (text, equals, ranges, lists, empty) and a global search, with fuzzy matching Facets The values a column holds under the other filters, with their counts, and its least and greatest numbers Grouping Rows grouped by one column or several, each group summed up (sum, mean, median, count, extent and more) Expanding rows Sub-rows and groups opened and closed, paged with the rest or inside their page Pages Pages of any size, with first, previous, next and last Row selection Rows, their sub-rows, a page or every filtered row, with a header checkbox's mixed state Row pinning Rows kept at the top or the bottom Columns Shown or hidden, reordered, pinned left or right, sized and resized, under header groups Simple grid A search field, a sort cycle and page buttons with their words, for rows of cells Using it use lory.datatable as dt columns = [dt.column['name', 'Name'], dt.column['age', 'Age', aggregate_with = 'mean']] people = [dt.row['p1', map[name = dt.words['Ada'], age = dt.number[36]]], dt.row['p2', map[name = dt.words['Alan'], age = dt.number[41]]], dt.row['p3', map[name = dt.words['Grace'], age = dt.number[29]]]] t = dt.new[columns, people] t = dt.sort_toggled[t, 'age', false] --- a press on Age's sort t = dt.search_set[t, dt.words['a']] --- what the search field holds t = dt.page_size_set[t, 25] m = dt.models[t] --- every row model, worked out once for r in m.page.rows --- the rows to draw, in order log['`r.id` `dt.shown[r.cells[\'name\']]` `dt.shown[r.cells[\'age\']]`'] log['`dt.page_count[t, m]` page'] A cell says what kind of value it holds: dt.words , dt.number , dt.truth , dt.date , dt.listed , or dt.missing[] for none. A missing value sorts after the others, and text that holds digits sorts as words and numbers ( item 9 before item 10 ). In a headset The table is drawn on a panel as on a screen: the controller's ray presses its headers, rows and page buttons, and the thumbstick scrolls its rows as a wheel does. Try it Open the data table example Not included yet Dragging columns to reorder them Rows loaded a page at a time from a server (the manual flags let a program do it itself)

Data grid and spreadsheet lory.datagrid puts cells to work on top of a data table : cells chosen, merged, edited, checked, pasted and worked out. A grid is drawn as one control, its header, rows and summary row painted together, with an edit bar over the cell being edited. Press a cell to focus it, drag or Shift-press to choose a rectangle, and Ctrl-press (Cmd on a Mac) to add or take away cells. The keys are a spreadsheet's: the arrows, Home and End, Page Up and Page Down, Ctrl+Home and Ctrl+End, Shift with each to extend the choice, Ctrl+A for every cell, Tab to move on, Enter or Space to edit, Escape to let an edit go, Delete and Backspace to clear, and Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V to copy and paste text a spreadsheet reads. Components Component What it does Data grid A table's rows as cells, focused, chosen and moved through by the keys Cell selection Rectangles of cells chosen by press, drag, Shift and Ctrl, counted, listed and copied Merged cells Neighbours holding the same value merged down a column, or across a row Cell editors Text, numbers, a list of choices and a box to tick, edited in the edit bar Rules Required, a number, at least and at most, one of the choices, unique, checked on every edit Relations One column turning another off, or choosing its choices Drafts Edits kept as drafts, the changed cells and rows known, saved together or one row at a time, or let go Summary row A column's sum, mean or other total in the footer Tree rows Groups that open and close, drawn as a tree Live grid Cells changed by a feed many times a second, the page, sort and choice kept, each change flashing up or down Spreadsheet Cells holding words or = formulas that read other cells ( =A0 + B1 ), worked out again as they change, with count, sum and mean of a range, cut, copy, paste, undo and redo Looks Three looks, among them striped rows and a clean one without lines Using it use sys use memory use lory use lory.gui use lory.datatable as dt use lory.datagrid as dg fn fresh[] columns = [dt.column['name', 'Name'], dt.column['hours', 'Hours']] people = [dt.row['p1', map[name = dt.words['Ada'], hours = dt.number[36]]], dt.row['p2', map[name = dt.words['Alan'], hours = dt.number[41]]]] g = dg.grid['people', dt.new[columns, people]] dg.specs_set[g, [dg.spec['hours', number = true, least = 0.0, most = 60.0, summary = 'sum']]] fn draw[frame] g = recall['grid', fresh[]] c = lory.begin[frame] shown = gui.show[c, gui.column[[dg.grid_view[g, 600.0, 300.0]]]] g = dg.handled[g, shown] --- presses, drags, keys and edits if g.copied ne '' shown.canvas = lory.copy[shown.canvas, g.copied] remember['grid', g] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] Set g.drafts = true to keep edits until dg.saved[g] . Copying leaves the text in g.copied , which lory.copy puts on the page's clipboard. In a headset The ray presses and drags across cells and the thumbstick scrolls the rows. An edit is typed on Lory's drawn keyboard into the edit bar. Try it Open the data grid example Not included yet Editors drawn inside the cell (edits use the edit bar) Date pickers and custom editors inside cells Pasting from the system clipboard by its own paste event Scrolling sideways with frozen columns, and dragging columns to resize them Several sheets in one spreadsheet

Charts Kite is Lory's charting package. kite.charts draws bar, line, scatter, bubble, pie, doughnut, polar area and radar charts from labels and datasets, with axes that fit their labels (linear, logarithmic, category, time and radial), a legend, titles and a tooltip. A chart is a view over your data, made each frame: put it in a gui tree with charts.drawn , or draw it straight onto the canvas with charts.shown_at . It can also be read from a JSON configuration of type , data and options with charts.of . Between frames Kite keeps what the reader did: the datasets the legend has hidden, the marks on their way to new values (they grow in as the chart first shows and move on when the data changes), what the pointer is over, and the place the arrow keys have reached. The pointer over a mark shows its tooltip, a press on a legend item hides or shows its dataset, and the chart tells your program as events of its id: hover , press , legend and current . Long lines are thinned to what the chart's width can show. Kite also draws financial charts: candles of six kinds, twenty-seven built-in indicators (moving averages, volume, MACD, RSI, Bollinger bands and more) in panes below or over the candles, axes that fit their labels (normal, percentage or logarithmic), a crosshair and tooltips, the high, low and last price marked, fifteen drawing tools, and a style for every part in a light or a dark theme. A drag scrolls it and glides on when let go, the wheel or a pinch zooms, a drag of an axis stretches it, a double click fits it again, and the arrow keys step a bar at a time. Components Component What it does Bar chart Bars by category, grouped or stacked, upright or across, with floating bars from a start to an end Line chart Lines through values, straight or curved, filled to their foot or to another line, with gaps Scatter and bubble charts Points placed by x and y, a bubble sized by its value Pie and doughnut charts Arcs of a whole, a doughnut with a hole of any size Polar area and radar charts Values round a centre on a radial axis Sparkline A small chart with no axes or legend, a line or bars, to sit beside words Legend and tooltip A legend whose items hide and show datasets; a tooltip at the marks under the pointer Candlestick chart Solid or hollow candles (or hollow only when rising or falling), OHLC bars or an area over time, kept between frames Indicators Twenty-seven built in, each in its own pane or over the candles Drawing tools Lines, rays, segments, price lines and channels, parallel lines, Fibonacci levels, annotations and tags, put down by clicks and dragged by their points Scanner card A dark card for a scanner: VWAP lines over the candles with a band above, the volume below, a percentage ladder from the previous close and zoom buttons Using it use sys use memory use lory use lory.gui use kite.charts struct Page [said] fn sales[] ch = charts.chart_of['sales', 'bar', ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr']] ch = charts.with_set[ch, charts.dataset['', 'This year', [65.0, 59.0, 80.0, 81.0]]] charts.with_set[ch, charts.dataset['line', 'Last year', [28.0, 48.0, 40.0, 19.0]]] fn draw[frame] a = recall['page', Page['Press a bar.']] c = lory.begin[frame] tree = gui.panel[[gui.heading['Sales'], charts.drawn[sales[], 0.0, 280.0], gui.note[a.said]]] shown = gui.show_at[c, tree, 24.0, 24.0, 560.0, gui.light[]] for e in shown.events if e.id eq 'sales' and e.act eq 'press' a.said = 'Pressed `e.words`.' remember['page', a] lory.end[shown.canvas] sys.frames[draw] A candlestick chart is a record kept between frames: use sys use lory use Maps The map package draws a map of the earth in any box of a Lory canvas: raster tiles from OpenStreetMap or any tile server, GeoJSON shapes in styles, markers with popups and tooltips, circles measured in metres, clusters of points and heatmaps, zoom buttons, a scale bar and the tiles' credit. A program writes use map , sets a map up once, and shows it each frame. The map is kept between frames under its id, and happened[id] says what the reader did to it. The reader drags the map and throws it, zooms it with the wheel about the pointer, with a double click (Shift zooms out), with two fingers or with a box drawn while holding Shift, and once the map has the keyboard, pans it with the arrow keys, zooms it with + and -, and closes a popup with Escape. A press opens a marker's or a shape's popup, and a pointer resting on a feature shows its tooltip. The program can fly the map from place to place along a smooth path that zooms out and in again, fit it to a box of places, or hold the view inside one. pressing it zooms in to where it comes apart Heatmap Points spread into heat, coloured from clear through blue, teal and yellow to red Zoom buttons, scale bar and credit The map's controls, each shown or hidden Device's place A blue dot in a circle of how sure it is, and a flight there Using it use sys use lory use map fn made[m] m = map.at[m, 48.8566, 2.3522, 5.0] m = map.tiles[m, map.openstreetmap[]] m = map.add_marker[m, 'paris', 48.8566, 2.3522, 'Paris'] m = map.add_circle[m, 'near', 48.8566, 2.3522, 50000.0, map.filled[map.style[], '#3388ff', 0.2]] m = map.bind_tooltip[m, 'near', '50 km about Paris'] map.add_geojson[m, 'road', '{"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[2.35, 48.86], [4.84, 45.76]]}', map.stroke[map.style[], '#c0392b', 3.0]] fn draw[frame] c = lory.begin[frame] m = map.of['world'] if not m.made m = made[m] c = map.show[c, m, 0.0, 0.0, lory.width[c], lory.height[c]] for told in map.happened['world'] if told.act eq 'click' and told.what eq 'paris' m = map.fly_to[map.of['world'], 48.8566, 2.3522, 12.0] map.keep[m] lory.end[c] sys.frames[draw] In a tree of Lory's controls the map is a drawn control, gui.drawn['world', 0.0, 600.0, 400.0, map.painter] , kept by the program with map.keep[m] before the tree is shown; its clicks and popups are among the tree's events. The parts it is made of ( map.geo for the projection and its arithmetic, map.camera for moves, map.grid for tiles, map.features for shapes and map.points for clusters and heat) can be used alone. In a headset The map is drawn on a panel, and the ray, where it meets the panel, is its pointer: the thumbstick zooms about the ray's point, and the trigger presses a marker, a shape, a cluster or a button, or drags the map while held. In AR the map stands in the room as a solid panel. 3D shapes and scenes Lory draws in three dimensions. lory.geometry builds shapes vertex by vertex: boxes, spheres, cylinders, tori and knots, capsules, lathes, the regular solids, tubes along curves, flat outlines with holes, extrusions with bevels, and surfaces found by marching cubes. lory.space holds those shapes on the page and draws them lit, through a camera, behind the flat drawing of panels and labels. It can also cast rays, test bounds and find what the pointer is over. lory.controls moves the camera or the things in the scene, and lory.flip turns a panel of controls in 3D to show its next side. Distances are in metres. On a screen, the camera orbits a point: drag to turn it and use the wheel to come nearer. A trackball turns the scene every way. A fly camera moves with W, A, S, D, R and F, rolls with Q and E, and turns with the arrow keys or by holding the pointer down. The pointer can take a thing and drag it over the plane that faces the eye. SVG path data read into them Edges and wireframes The edges where faces meet at more than an angle, or every triangle's edges, drawn as lines Marching cubes A surface found in a sampled field, such as a group of balls Meshes and forms Shapes held on the page and drawn as triangles, lines or points, with a colour for each vertex Looks Plain and physically based surfaces, plus unlit, matte, glossy and facing-coloured materials; dashes, points, blending, pictures and alpha cut-outs Lamps Ambient, sky-and-ground, directional, point and spot lights, with shadows from one lamp Fog Linear fog or a haze that thickens with depth Cameras and views Perspective and orthographic lenses, a camera that orbits a point, several views side by side Copies Many copies of one shape drawn at once, each placed and coloured on its own Levels of detail The mesh a thing's distance asks for, chosen from finer and coarser ones Picking Rays from the pointer or a controller, and what they hit: triangles, lines and points Bounds and culling Boxes and spheres that hold a shape, and whether a camera sees it Helpers Axes, a grid on the ground, a box's outline and an arrow Fly, trackball and drag controls A camera flown through the scene or turned every way, and things dragged by the pointer Flip shape A panel of sides that turns like a cube or a card to show the next Using it use sys use lory use lory.space use lory.geometry use lory.controls fn draw[frame] c = lory.begin[frame] if not space.made['knot'] c = space.mesh_form[c, 'knot', geometry.space_form[geometry.torus_knot[1.0, 0.4, 64, 8, 2.0, 3.0]]] c = space.mesh[c, 'ground', space.ground[8.0, 8.0]] lens_of = space.lens[50.0, space.proportion[c], 0.1, 100.0] cam = controls.trackball[c, 'view', lens_of, [0.0, 1.5, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0, 8.0]] c = space.through[c, cam, space.daylight[]] c = space.lamps[c, [space.ambient[lory.white[], 0.3], space.directional[lory.white[], 2.0, [2.0, 4.0, 3.0], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]]]] c = space.draw[c, 'ground', lory.identity[], space.plain[lory.hex['#9ca3af']]] c = space.draw[c, 'knot', lory.translation[0.0, 1.5, 0.0], space.standard[lory.hex['#e8590c'], 0.2, 0.4]] lory.end[c] sys.frames[draw] In a headset A scene is drawn for each eye, and the camera becomes the reader's head. The floor is at 0 and the reader stands at the origin. The controller's ray picks things and its trigger takes them. The left stick walks and the right one turns ( space.walk ), and space.stand_at teleports. In AR, the room shows through wherever nothing is drawn. Try it Open the 3D scenes example The 3D shapes example shows every shape, and the first 3D scene is a sphere over a ground in under fifty lines.

3D model files lory.models reads 3D model files into Lory's geometries and writes models back out. It reads OBJ (with its MTL's materials), STL (text and binary), PLY (text and binary, either byte order), XYZ and PCD point clouds (PCD in text, binary or compressed binary), VTK's legacy text form and OFF. It writes OBJ, STL (text and binary), PLY (text and binary) and glTF 2.0. A program writes use lory.models , reads a file's bytes into a model, and draws it in a lory.space scene with the pointer turning the camera. A model is its parts in the file's order, each a mesh of triangles, lines or points, with its colours in linear light and its materials. A reader never stops the program: a file it cannot read gives a model of no parts whose failure says why. format ascii 1.0
element vertex 3
property float x
property float y
property float z

property list uchar int vertex_indices
end_header
0 0 0
1 0 0
0 1 0

In a headset A model is drawn in the room like any other part of a lory.space scene, so it can stand beside a page at whatever size the program gives it, and the controller's ray presses the buttons of the panel that goes with it. Sound The sound package makes audio in your program itself, sample by sample: synths and a sampler, envelopes, oscillators, noise and players, filters, effects and dynamics, sound placed around the listener, a transport that says which notes fall when, analysers and meters, and controls to play it all with. use sound and the modules you need: sound.signal , sound.envelope , sound.transport , sound.source , sound.filter , sound.synth , sound.effect , sound.dynamics , sound.channel , sound.analysis and sound.ui . A sound is a value: a rate and one or two channels of samples. Nothing is a live audio graph; everything is rendered ahead and handed to the page with sound.play , which starts it a given number of seconds from now. A program that plays as it goes, a sequencer or a keyboard, renders each note when it is due and hands it over a little ahead ( transport.clock and transport.due keep that lead). Time is written in notation ( 4n a quarter note, 8t a triplet, 1m a bar, 2:1:0 bars, beats and sixteenths) and pitch by name ( C4 , F#5 ) or MIDI number. The controls take a mouse, a touch or a headset's ray; a knob also turns by the arrows, Page Up and Page Down, Home and End. C5', '8n', '0'] hits = for f in transport.fired[tr, 0.0, 0.5] synth.hit[f.time, sound.hz[f.value], 0.1, 0.8] tune = synth.played[synth.fm_synth[], hits, 22050.0] effect.applied[effect.with_wet[effect.feedback_delay[], 0.5], tune, 0.0] --- in a frame: the page starts the tune 50 ms from now fn draw[c] sound.play[c, tune_of[], 0.05] In a headset The listener can be the reader's head ( channel.listener_of[c] ), so a placed sound stays where it is in the room as the head turns. Reactive state A gallery of small examples about state that changes and what follows from it: a count moved by a timer, a list kept between visits, a form checked as it is typed, a clock redrawn every frame, a lookup that loads and may fail, pages chosen by an address. A menu of them runs down the side, the one chosen beside it, and a switch under the menu turns the page light or dark. Each example is a module that knows only Lory: its state made fresh , moved on before a frame is drawn (timers, waits, animations, answers that come due), drawn as a tree of lory.gui controls, and moved by what the reader did after .
